title: What to Do After a Storm Damaged Tree on Your Property
excerpt: A storm damaged tree can look fine and still be a serious risk. Here's how to tell what needs emergency attention, what can wait, and what to document for your insurance claim.

seoTitle: What to Do After a Storm Damaged Tree on Your Property
seoDescription: A storm damaged tree can look stable and still be dangerous. Here's how to assess it, what to avoid, and how to document it for insurance.
bodyMarkdown:
A storm damaged tree can look fine from the porch and still be one gust away from coming down. If a storm just came through your part of North Georgia and left a tree leaning, cracked, or dropping limbs, what you do in the next day matters — both for keeping your family safe and for what your insurance company will need later. Here's a practical walkthrough of what to check, what to leave alone, and when to call someone.

## Assessing a Storm Damaged Tree: What to Look For

Start from a distance, not underneath the tree. Look at the whole shape first: is the tree leaning more than it used to, even slightly? A new lean, especially with soil heaving or cracking at the base, often means the root system has partially failed — that's one of the more dangerous signs, because the tree can fail without any more wind at all.

Next, look up into the canopy for hanging limbs that didn't fully break off — arborists call these widowmakers for a reason, and they can fall hours or days after the storm with no warning. Check the trunk for new vertical cracks or splits, which weaken the tree's structural integrity even if the crown looks mostly intact. If a large limb tore away and left an exposed wound on the trunk, that's worth noting for later but isn't itself an emergency.

If any of these signs point to a tree that could come down onto the house, a driveway, or power lines, treat it as urgent and keep everyone — including pets — away from that part of the yard until it's been looked at.

## When to Call for Emergency Tree Removal

Not every storm-damaged tree needs same-day attention, but some situations genuinely do: a tree leaning onto a structure, one resting on power lines, or one blocking the only way in or out of your driveway. For those, our [emergency tree service](/emergency-tree-service) crews handle exactly this kind of call, and can usually get someone out faster than you'd expect for genuinely hazardous situations.

For a tree that's damaged but stable — a broken limb high up, some split bark, nothing threatening to fall — it's still worth getting a professional opinion within a few days rather than waiting. A [tree removal](/tree-removal) or [tree trimming](/tree-trimming) assessment now can catch problems before the next storm turns a manageable repair into an emergency.

## What Not to Do

Don't get on a ladder with a chainsaw. Storm-damaged trees hold tension in ways that aren't obvious from the ground — a limb that looks stable can be under enough spring-load that cutting it releases it violently. This is one of the leading causes of serious injury after storms, and it's not a place to save money by doing it yourself.

Also don't assume power lines near a downed limb are dead just because the power's out at your house. Treat any tree touching a line as energized until the utility company confirms otherwise, and call them directly rather than trying to move branches away from lines yourself.

## Documenting Storm Damage for Insurance

Before anything gets cut or hauled away, take photos and video from multiple angles — the whole tree, the point of failure, and any damage to your house, fence, or car. Most homeowner policies cover storm-damaged tree removal when the tree hit something insured, though coverage for removing a tree that fell in the yard without hitting anything varies by policy, so it's worth a call to your agent before you assume either way.

Keep any invoice from the tree service as part of your claim, and don't discard large debris until your adjuster has had a chance to see it if a claim is likely. The [Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org) has a clear breakdown of how tree damage claims typically work if you want more detail before you call your agent.

## Preventing the Next Storm Damaged Tree

Once the immediate damage is handled, it's worth thinking about the trees you didn't lose this time. Regular [tree trimming](/tree-trimming) reduces the sail effect that catches wind and brings down weakly attached limbs, and it's far cheaper than emergency work after the fact. Trees with existing decay, poor structure, or a history of dropping limbs are the ones most likely to fail in the next storm, so an assessment now — before spring storm season builds again — is worth the time.

For weather tracking during an active storm, the [National Weather Service](https://www.weather.gov) is the most reliable source for real-time warnings in North Georgia, and the [Georgia Forestry Commission](https://www.gatrees.org) and [International Society of Arboriculture](https://www.isa-arbor.com) both publish good background on storm-damaged tree risk if you want to understand more about how trees fail. The [Tree Care Industry Association](https://www.tcia.org) is also a solid place to check credentials before hiring anyone for storm cleanup — a busy season after a storm tends to bring out crews who aren't properly insured.
